questions.question: Malaria is caused by a protozoon of which genus?
questions.explanation: Malaria is caused by protozoa of the genus Plasmodium. Four species naturally infect humans: P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale.

questions.question: Malaria is transmitted to humans through the bite of which mosquito?
questions.explanation: Only the female Anopheles mosquito transmits malaria. She requires a blood meal for egg development, and it is during this feeding that she injects sporozoites into the human host.

questions.question: How many Plasmodium species are naturally parasitic in humans?
questions.explanation: Four Plasmodium species naturally infect humans — P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale. A fifth (P. knowlesi) primarily infects monkeys and occasionally humans in Southeast Asia.

questions.question: Which is not a human Plasmodium species?
questions.explanation: P. canis is a parasite of dogs, not a human Plasmodium species. The four human species are P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale.

questions.question: Malaria is characterized by fever, anaemia, and which condition?
questions.explanation: The classical triad of malaria is periodic fever, anaemia, and splenomegaly (enlarged spleen). Jaundice can occur in severe cases but is not part of the classical triad.

questions.question: Which Plasmodium species causes malignant tertian malaria?
questions.explanation: P. falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria — the most severe form. It is responsible for the vast majority of malaria deaths worldwide.

questions.question: P. falciparum is described as the most what of the human plasmodia?
questions.explanation: P. falciparum is the most virulent of the human plasmodia, capable of causing severe complications including cerebral malaria and death within days if untreated.

questions.question: The exoerythrocytic schizont of P. falciparum grows in which cells?
questions.explanation: The exoerythrocytic (pre-erythrocytic) stage of P. falciparum develops in liver cells (hepatocytes) before releasing merozoites into the bloodstream.

questions.question: Relapses do not occur in P. falciparum malaria, but what may follow remission?
questions.explanation: P. falciparum has no persistent liver stage, so true relapses cannot occur. However, recrudescences — recurrence from surviving blood-stage parasites — may follow clinical remission.

questions.question: P. falciparum merozoites can invade erythrocytes of what age?
questions.explanation: Unlike P. vivax (which invades only reticulocytes) and P. malariae (which prefers aging cells), P. falciparum invades erythrocytes of any age, leading to much higher parasite densities.

questions.question: Infected erythrocytes in P. falciparum develop which structures?
questions.explanation: P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes develop Maurer's clefts — irregular, red-staining patches in the cytoplasm visible on stained films. Schuffner's dots are seen in P. vivax and P. ovale.

questions.question: Sequestration in P. falciparum malaria means withdrawal of what?
questions.explanation: Sequestration is the adhesion of parasitized erythrocytes to the endothelial lining of deep blood vessels, effectively withdrawing them from circulation. This is a hallmark of falciparum malaria and contributes to organ damage.

questions.question: Rosettes in falciparum malaria form when infected cells bind to what?
questions.explanation: Rosetting is the binding of infected erythrocytes to uninfected red cells, forming a rosette-like cluster. This contributes to microvascular obstruction.

questions.question: The early ring-stage trophozoite of P. falciparum is the smallest of any what?
questions.explanation: The ring-stage trophozoite of P. falciparum is the smallest of all human Plasmodium species — often described as "delicate" and easy to miss on microscopy.

questions.question: P. vivax is the causative agent of which malaria?
questions.explanation: P. vivax causes benign tertian malaria, named for the milder course and the 48-hour (tertian) fever cycle.

questions.question: Fever paroxysms in P. vivax malaria typically recur every how many hours?
questions.explanation: The 48-hour cycle reflects the duration of erythrocytic schizogony in P. vivax. The paroxysm recurs every third day by inclusive counting, hence "tertian."

questions.question: Sporozoites of P. vivax may remain in liver cells as what?
questions.explanation: P. vivax (and P. ovale) form dormant hypnozoites in the liver. These can reactivate months or years later, causing true relapses.

questions.question: Relapses of vivax malaria can occur up to how many years after infection?
questions.explanation: Relapses of P. vivax malaria can occur up to 8 years after the initial infection, due to the reactivation of hypnozoites in the liver.

questions.question: Merozoites of P. vivax invade only which erythrocytes?
questions.explanation: P. vivax merozoites invade only reticulocytes (young red cells). This limits parasite density, which is one reason vivax malaria is generally milder than falciparum.

questions.question: The characteristic stippling in P. vivax infected erythrocytes is called what?
questions.explanation: Schuffner's dots are fine, pinkish-red stippling seen throughout the cytoplasm of P. vivax-infected erythrocytes on stained films.

questions.question: Erythrocytic schizogony of P. vivax takes about how long?
questions.explanation: The erythrocytic cycle of P. vivax takes about 48 hours, matching the 48-hour fever periodicity.

questions.question: P. malariae is the causative organism of which malaria?
questions.explanation: P. malariae causes quartan malaria, named for its 72-hour fever cycle — every fourth day by inclusive counting.

questions.question: Paroxysms in P. malariae malaria occur every how many hours?
questions.explanation: The 72-hour cycle reflects the longer erythrocytic schizogony of P. malariae.

questions.question: Merozoites of P. malariae apparently invade which erythrocytes?
questions.explanation: P. malariae merozoites preferentially invade aging erythrocytes. This is why the parasite density remains low and the infection tends to be chronic.

questions.question: Recrudescences of quartan malaria can recur up to how many years?
questions.explanation: Recrudescences of P. malariae malaria have been documented up to 53 years after the initial infection — the longest of any human malaria species.

questions.question: P. malariae is the most important cause of which condition?
questions.explanation: Because P. malariae persists in the blood at low, often undetectable levels for years, it is the most common cause of transfusion-transmitted malaria.

questions.question: P. ovale causes which type of malaria?
questions.explanation: P. ovale causes ovale malaria, also called mild tertian malaria. It is milder than P. vivax and largely confined to West Africa.

questions.question: P. ovale is the rarest of how many human malaria parasites?
questions.explanation: P. ovale is the rarest of the four human malaria parasites. It occurs mainly in West Africa.

questions.question: Pathogenesis of malaria involves destruction of large numbers of what?
questions.explanation: The destruction of large numbers of erythrocytes during schizogony causes anaemia, jaundice, and haemoglobinuria — the core pathogenic mechanism of malaria.

questions.question: Intense haemolysis in P. falciparum infection may cause what?
questions.explanation: Blackwater fever is a complication of falciparum malaria in which massive intravascular haemolysis causes haemoglobinuria, producing dark-red to black urine.

questions.question: The malaria pigment produced from host haemoglobin is called what?
questions.explanation: Haemozoin (malaria pigment) is a dark brown-black crystalline pigment produced by the parasite as a by-product of haemoglobin digestion. It accumulates in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

questions.question: Enlargement of the liver is known as what?
questions.explanation: Hepatomegaly is enlargement of the liver. Splenomegaly is enlargement of the spleen. Both occur in chronic malaria.

questions.question: Margination in malaria refers to arrangement of parasitized erythrocytes in what?
questions.explanation: Margination is the accumulation of parasitized erythrocytes along the walls of blood vessels (especially capillaries and venules), contributing to microvascular obstruction.

questions.question: Clinical features of malaria include periodic fever, splenomegaly, anaemia, and what?
questions.explanation: Leucopaenia (reduced white blood cell count) is a common feature of malaria, alongside periodic fever, splenomegaly, and anaemia.

questions.question: Falciparum malaria is always described as what?
questions.explanation: Falciparum malaria is always described as dangerous — it can progress rapidly to severe complications and death without prompt treatment.

questions.question: The intrinsic incubation period for falciparum malaria is how many days?
questions.explanation: The intrinsic incubation period for P. falciparum malaria is 11 to 14 days — the time from sporozoite inoculation to the appearance of clinical symptoms.

questions.question: The typical paroxysm of benign tertian malaria begins with what?
questions.explanation: A malarial paroxysm has three stages: a cold stage with rigor (shivering), a hot stage with fever, and a sweating stage. It begins with rigor.

questions.question: The sweating stage of a malarial paroxysm lasts how many hours?
questions.explanation: The sweating stage of a malarial paroxysm lasts 2 to 3 hours. The patient sweats profusely as the fever breaks, and the temperature returns to normal.

questions.question: In quartan malaria, the total duration of a paroxysm averages how many hours?
questions.explanation: In P. malariae (quartan) malaria, the paroxysm averages 11 hours total. This is longer than in the other species.

questions.question: Nephrosis in chronic malaria occurs especially in which infection?
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome is a recognised complication of chronic P. malariae infection, especially in West African children.

questions.question: Cerebral malaria is characterized by headache, coma, and what else?
questions.explanation: Cerebral malaria is characterized by severe headache, hyperpyrexia (very high fever), and coma. It is a medical emergency.

questions.question: Pulmonary oedema in severe falciparum malaria may result from over administration of what?
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic pulmonary oedema in falciparum malaria often results from over-administration of intravenous fluids, causing fluid overload.

questions.question: Algid malaria is a rapid development of what?
questions.explanation: Algid malaria is a rare, rapidly progressive form of severe falciparum malaria characterized by shock, hypothermia, and circulatory collapse.

questions.question: Blackwater fever is characterized by dark-red to black what?
questions.explanation: Blackwater fever produces dark-red to black urine (haemoglobinuria) due to massive intravascular haemolysis.

questions.question: Hypoglycaemia in falciparum malaria means reduced concentration of what?
questions.explanation: Hypoglycaemia is a common and dangerous complication of severe falciparum malaria, especially in children and pregnant women. Blood glucose concentration is reduced.

questions.question: Microscopy is currently described as which method for detecting malaria parasites?
questions.explanation: Microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films remains the gold standard for malaria diagnosis — it allows species identification and parasite quantification.

questions.question: Clinical diagnosis of malaria is very sensitive but has low what?
questions.explanation: Clinical diagnosis (based on symptoms alone) is sensitive — it catches most real cases — but has low specificity, meaning it also misdiagnoses many non-malaria fevers as malaria.

questions.question: Microscopy allows parasite densities to be quantified from the ratio of parasites to what?
questions.explanation: Parasite density is quantified by counting parasites against leucocytes (in thick films) or erythrocytes (in thin films). This gives the parasite count per microlitre.

questions.question: Prophylactic antimalarial drugs include chloroquine/proguanil, doxycycline, and what?
questions.explanation: Atovaquone/proguanil (Malarone) is a common prophylactic regimen, along with chloroquine/proguanil and doxycycline.

questions.question: Classical larvicides include Paris green, larvicidal oils, and what?
questions.explanation: Polystyrene beads are a modern larvicide — they form a floating layer on water surfaces that prevents mosquito larvae from breathing. Paris green and larvicidal oils are older larvicides.
